7.6.m:
“Why do you worry so exceedingly, sinless one? Whence comes this anxiety of yours? / Since you are a master, my son, this is not fitting for you.”
Sukeśa said:
“Having heard from you about the suffering born of living beings' karma, / I wonder how there might be a means for their liberation.”
The ancestors said:
“Without regard to its exhaustion, my son, their liberation cannot be found, / [namely,] of their own actions performed in this world; and that exhaustion is considered [to come only] from experiencing the fruits.
And that experiencing [of fruits] in hell is inevitably performed by the living being; / nor can those hell-dwellers be rescued without the exhaustion of karma.
Indeed, wise men should not undertake those tasks that are impossible, / just as swimming across the ocean meets you with death.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed in this manner, that radiant [sage], filled with deep love, / bowed down and said to those ancestors: “Do not disregard me, your son!

Then, having taken leave of them, that great-souled leader of the Gaṇas / entered the ocean waters and, staying beneath the water,
pure-minded, motionless, and deeply absorbed in meditation, recited the Rudra [hymns]. / As that great-souled one, endowed with yoga, was reciting,
the entire threefold world, O Vyāsa, was heated by his austerity. / Thereupon, all the gods spoke to the Grandfather [Brahmā]:
“O Lord, why are we all burning helplessly? / Whose power of austerity is this? Whose yoga is such?
Who is this, O tiger among gods, that performs such terrible austerity? / Before it burns in this way, and before he becomes angry,
fulfill all his desires, O Lord!” / Addressed thus by those gods, the blessed best of deities
said: “Do not fear! He is not someone objectionable. / He is that great-souled leader of the Gaṇas belonging to the God of gods.

and likewise, one composed in mind who protects a cow that is stuck in mud, / fallen, or bereft of strength, he does not go there at all; // 8
and he who with supreme meditation constantly worships / the Great Lord with devotion and inner feeling, he does not go there at all. // 9
For others, however, worldly rebirth certainly occurs; there is no doubt. / Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas and Vedāṅgas do not go there; // 10
devoted to the six duties, O Vyāsa, steadfast in their own dharma, / endowed with austerity and purity, compassionate, firm in their vows; // 11

Those whose livelihood is uninterrupted and who worship the gods and brahmins / do not see hell; they are declared to go to heaven. (14)
Śūdras who are devoted to the three [higher] castes and devoid of arrogance, / and who especially attend upon brahmins constantly, (15) / do not see hell; when dead, they go to a good destination. / And among all four castes, those mortals who [worship] Śiva with sincere devotion, (16)
having dedicated their actions and states to Śarva, devoted and ever steadfast, / do not go to hell; they attain the supreme state. (17)
And those who, having built a temple, worship the God of gods, / deliver even other ancestors from hell. (18)
Those by whom lotus-ponds, reservoirs, and lakes have been dug, / and groves of trees planted, indeed do not go to those [hells]. (19)

And those who constantly protect the twice-born and other afflicted beings / do not go to those [hells]. (20) / And those who are never prone to anger, who worship the gods and brahmins, / and are ever devoted to giving, do not go to a lower destination. (21)
Endowed with truthful speech, free from wicked undertakings, / and observing the practices of their own duty, they do not see hell. (22)
Therefore, one devoted to worshipping the liṅga is liberated from everything. / One who is meditative at all times, or who, being pure, chants [the names of Śiva's] gaṇas, (23) / and a yogi, even while doing all sins, is not tainted.
For women, however, the supreme god is always the husband. (24) / [Variant readings: 25. satataṃ na vyavacchinnā, in MS kha. 26. pūjane, in MSS ka, gha. 27. goptā gobrāhmaṇasya ca, in MS kha. 28. varṇatraye, in MS kha. 29. ye nityamupasevate, in MS ka. 30. na te, in MS kha. 31. narakān,]

The woman who, even when her husband has died, desires no other man in her mind, / and whatever merit she acquires, assigns it all to her husband— / that woman does not go to any hells even in thought. (27)
She does not undergo terrible worldly existence at all. / For other [women], however, there is no doubt regarding hell, O you of good vows. (28)
Sanatkumāra said:
Having thus favored Sukeśa, the God whose mount is the bull / […] went to the hermitage of Kāṣṭhakūṭa. / He bestowed his grace on that brahmin Kāṣṭhakūṭa, whose wealth was austerity. (29)
Vyāsa said:
What was the austerity of that noble brahmin, O Lord, / and after how long a time did he obtain a boon from Maheśvara? (30)
Whose son was he? Whose grandson? What was the name of that most virtuous man? / I wish to hear this auspicious matter recounted in detail, O Lord. (31)

did not obtain a son with her, and was overcome by old age. / Afflicted with grief, he, skilled in speech, said to his wife: (34) / 'Through a son, men desire the worlds, and they become free of debt. / I have reached old age, and no son of mine is seen. (35)
Therefore, permitted by me, O auspicious woman, approach / some man of my clan for the sake of a son; bowing with joined palms, I implore you.' (36)
Suyaśas said:
Never have I heard such a thing, nor has such a thing been spoken by you, O sinless one! / How could a woman like me consider such a deed even in her mind? (37)
Born into the lineage of Atri, and having entered the lineage of Gautama, / how could one such as I do that which is condemned by the virtuous? (38)
Through austerity one should seek wealth, lives, and pleasures, / sons, family, and worlds. Perform austerity, O great sage! (39)
For indeed, by austerity the son Parāśara was obtained by Śakti, / and through his own austerity the great sage Aurva [was obtained] by Cyavana.

This exertion of yours is entirely in vain; you have no son, O sinless one." / Thus spoken to, despondent and despairing of the birth of a son,
he resolved on death, [deciding] not to return to his own home.
He gathered a pile of wood and, seizing fire, deeply grieved,

7.6.m:
Bhūmanyu said:
"Service to parents, O son, is of two kinds, conformable to dharma, / which must be performed with effort by an exceedingly noble son:
service to the physical body belonging to this world, and that which yields merit in the next, / by which the ancestors cross over and attain imperishable desires. / In this regard, this-worldly [service] is not desired by us so much as what is beneficial for the hereafter. / Therefore, practice whatever deed belongs to the hereafter.
Go, study both Śruti and Smṛti of noble deeds." / Suyaśā said:
"As this father of yours who knows himself tells you, my son, / so act, that god Bhava may become a granter of boons to you. / In my womb, O highly wise one, you were carried with sorrow, / and similarly obtained through many hardships for the accomplishment of every aim.

7.6.m:
Sent off by the two of them, he then went toward Cyavana, / like an oblation properly offered through Ṛg and Yajus going toward Varuṇa.
Reaching him, he was made successful by him who was well pleased, / like a leading mantra attaining its share with the gods. / Then, when that son had departed, the father met his appointed end. / Thereupon, having completed his learning, the very righteous Kāṣṭhakūṭa approached,
and saw his mother, wretched like a lotus pond bereft of water, / like a night deprived of the moon, like royal fortune devoid of authority, / weeping, her eyes full of tears, lamenting, deeply grieved.
Kāṣṭhakūṭa, having seen her overwhelmed with sorrow, / like Jayanta seeing Paulomī when Śakra was lost, spoke this: / Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"I have already heard this, and the funeral rites have indeed been performed. / Do not fix your mind on grief; this is the eternal law.

"All the Vedas have been studied by me together with their limbs, secondary limbs, and details, / as well as all the secondary Vedas and the supreme self entirely.
Whatever is to be known by men, all that is indeed known; / what is to be heard has all been heard, and yogins have been revered.
Delighting through this very preeminence, endowed with joy, / protect me, O lady of great courage, just as Gāyatrī ever [protects] the sacrifice."

Sanatkumāra said: / Having heard those truthful words of that great-souled one, his mother, / weeping with even greater sorrow, spoke to him: / Suyaśā said:
"Son, my sorrow is not that he died; this is agreed: / this is ordained for all creatures possessing a mortal nature.
And he, great-souled and endowed with austerity, had accomplished his purpose; / there is nothing at all to be mourned by us on his account here. / I grieve for myself, O son, who have been abandoned without him; / longing for your return, I did not die right after him.
Neither wealth, nor pleasures, nor kinsmen, nor sons, nor friends / matter to women where the husband resides. / If there is a husband, then there is everything; there is nothing without a husband.

7.6.m:
For he said to me many times: 'Kāṣṭhakūṭa will come here, / having completed his learning; then I shall choose an auspicious daughter-in-law for him. / This daughter of Odala of the Kaśyapa gotra is exceedingly virtuous; / I will choose that girl of good vows for Kāṣṭhakūṭa.
Then I shall see that son of firm vows with his wife, / and seeing him accompanied by a wife, I will set up the sacred fires. / When, pleased by the grasping of the bride's hand for my son, / shall I perform many auspicious things in mind and speech?'
Thus, of him who had such desires, of him who had a son, / of him who had a beloved son, it did not come to pass; this burns me, O son! / And you were told by me before, as you were going to his presence: / 'May we see you while both of us are alive!' And that did not happen thus.
Surely my heart today is made of the essence of diamond, since it does not split,
in that I, an unchaste wife, look upon you here again, my son, without him!"

"Alas, father, on account of me of evil mind, ignorant of righteousness! / […] / Where have you gone? Together with your wife, you do not speak to me today.
Were I not directed by you, as if delighted: 'Go, study'? / I, that very person, having studied, have arrived today; why do you not speak to me? / Indeed, obtained by your austerity and supreme concentration, / I am a son [born] from Rudra, the God of gods; why do you not speak?
What wrong was done by me, O sinless father, to you along with your wife, / that you, arriving together with mother, do not welcome me firmly at all? / Alas, you were killed by me alone, a wicked son, an evil-minded one! / I think this realm is without a king, since it does not execute me, a patricide!"

Then, having seen the Lord of gods resembling the rising sun, / he fell at his feet delighted, and spoke this in a clear voice:
Kāṣṭhakūṭa said:
"O Lord, my mother and father have been joined with death; / may both of them live, O God; this is the boon I desire."
The God of gods said:
"Both of them have entered a dreadful hell, afflicted by death; / they cannot be restored to life again. Choose another [boon] from Me."

And all these seers, ascetics in this hermitage, / having become your attendants, shall become lords of the gaṇas.
Imperishable and undecaying, endowed with the power of great yoga, / and equal to you in sovereign power they shall become, without doubt.
And this your father, my son, Bhūmanyu, together with his wife, / having become your attendant, is present here equal to you.
And I grant that divine Śveta mountain, adorned with aerial chariots, / moving at will, resembling heaven as an abode.”
Sanatkumāra said:
Then that blessed Lord, having favored that mighty one, / went once more to Mandara, and he too went to his desired region.
While the Goddess, engaged in austerity, remained on her father's peak, / so long did the God do all this that has been told.
The man who hears this deed of the God of gods, / or causes brahmins to hear it, would not meet with an evil state.

7.6.m:
And how did she, the source of hundreds of boons, obtain a boon? / I desire all this to be told, O best of brahmins!
Sanatkumāra said:
Hear, as time passed, the Goddess's most difficult austerity: / being pure, folding her hands in reverence, and steadying her mind,
directing her eyes and her mind toward the sun, / she stood unblinking like a wooden image, as if bound to a tree.
Gazing at the sun, she turned along with its course; / standing on one foot with raised arms, she became breathless indeed.
For a divine thousand years she remained motionless like a stone, / Rudrāṇī accompanied only by a tiger, engaged in austerity, firm in her sacred vow.
Nor did she suffer fatigue, nor loss of strength; / just as before, that Goddess stood devoted to austerity.
By the power of her austerity, the whole world, stationary and moving, / stood distressed, as though struck down by non-existence.

7.6.m:
The sun shone with diminished radiance; the moon did not shine; / the luminaries turned dark; and the perfected beings did not travel in the sky.
The garlands of the gods withered, and their aerial chariots fell; / even in heaven there was no happiness for them, and anxiety arose.
All directions began to smoke, and indeed the entire triple world; / the course of the Vidyādharas was broken, and their weapons blazed.
Deer and tigers and lions, cats, owls, and mice, / snakes and mongooses roamed gathered in one place.

Then the gods assembled and said to one another: / “This reversal of this triple world is not seen to happen without a cause.
There must be a great reason here; this cannot be without cause. / Therefore, not knowing all this reversal,
why do we stand here agitated? Let us go into the presence of Brahmā!” / Having spoken thus, all those gods, with Bṛhaspati at their head,
went to the abode of Virāj and bowed down before Brahmā. / Honored duly by Brahmā, they sat down according to their rank.

Asked by him the reason for their coming, afflicted with grief in their hearts, they said: / “O Blessed One, the whole truth of the worlds is evident before the all-pervading Lord.
"Why has this world now become disordered? Tell us, O lord!"
Having heard those words of those frightened ones, the knower of all yoga,
spoke this sweet, gentle, and solemn speech:
"This Goddess Rudrāṇī, born of Himavat, the sustainer of the world,
with disciplined self performs tapas, having resorted to unwavering yoga.
Now indeed a thousand divine years have passed for her in samādhi,
as well as two hundred years and another hundred autumns.
As she performs tapas through yoga, O gods, this is the power
of her tapas, by which disorder has come upon the worlds."
The gods said:
"If this fear of a great calamity is through her power,
she may burn the worlds even further from this; therefore, restrain her!

Compassion, mercy, charity, and faith along with modesty, / all stood beside the seers, while the sacrificial fee stood beside sacrifice. / Then whatever gods dwelt in Brahmā's world, / having quickly mounted on all sides, took their places.
When all of them had thus completely boarded that aerial chariot / and all were comfortably seated, Brahmā set it in motion. / Impelled by that knower of yoga moving at the forefront, that supreme great aerial chariot, going everywhere, / departed by its power, following thought, just as the mind itself [is moved] by the Creator of all.
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, entitled 'The Departure of Brahmā', in the bestowal of the goddess's boons, in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then in that aerial chariot, the wise, four-faced Creator of all / went to Mount Mandara, which has caves of varied jewels.
Reaching that vast, peerless, and exceedingly brilliant [mountain], / delightful to behold from afar, he saw it and addressed those present in the assembly:

7.6.m:
Upon entering this, the fortune of the gods' sacrifice does not depart, / nor does victory in battles, nor the very great dharma. / This peerless luster was created by him with his mind;
for there is no dwelling comparable to this in this cosmic egg.
Having entered this, the righteous person experiences no further sorrow, / nor does he attain rebirth, for he is ever endowed with supreme sovereignty. / This is eternally indescribable through yoga even by yogins; / how then could any other person, however great, describe it?
Struck in fury by the wind of our aerial chariot, / this [mountain] rises together with the mountain, like the peak of the Vindhya.
This stands blocking the path of our aerial chariot, / upward, across, and below, by the fiery energy of the God of gods.
Creating this blinding darkness, this cloud, the source of life itself, / bearing a garland with a thunderbolt raised in hand, approaches roaring loudly."

the Lord of gods, spoke thus to Nandin standing at the doorway: / 'This Brahmā has come here in an aerial chariot to see me. / Tell [him]: "The business for which you have come here is known to me. / Carry it out and depart quickly, for the time for it has arrived."'
Sanatkumāra said:
Thus addressed by Rudra, Nandin, the leader of the Pramathas, / standing right at the door, spoke thus to Brahmā in the aerial chariot:
Nandin said: / 'You are known to the Blessed One, as is the business for which you have come. / Accomplish that quickly indeed; the time for it is at hand.'
Sanatkumāra said: / Then, having made mental obeisance to Śambhu, / he circumambulated Mandara and departed. / Having passed completely around Mount Mandara, that noble-minded one / came to Jambudvīpa by way of Śākadvīpa.
Beheld by the gods and by sages with restrained vows, / he approached the Himalaya, the foremost of mountains, and said: [21]

7.6.m:
“Behold the power of the Goddess’s austerity and noble conduct! / For having seen this peak, we shall not see rebirth. // 25 //”
Speaking thus, the four-faced [Brahmā] in his aerial chariot, / accompanied by all the seers, arrived at the gateway to the peak. // 26 // / There, Rudra’s attendants, with raised weapons in their hands, / approached him menacingly, crying out: “Halt! Halt!” // 27
Brahmā spoke to them in gentle words, preceded by soothing words, / praising them all, with folded hands and a calm mind. // 28 // / Brahmā said:
“You are all great-souled, endowed with sovereign power, / imperishable, immortal, and truly unhindered, // 29 // / possessing the power of great yoga, invincible to anyone in battle. / Who could surpass you, O supreme lords, even Śakra? // 30
Having come here from Mandara by the command of the God of gods / to grant a boon to the Goddess, let permission be granted to me.” // 31 // / The lords of the gaṇas said:

First give a boon to this tiger; after that you will give a boon to me. / Today a thousand years have passed as he has stood before me, // 9 // / meditating, unblinking, with ears erect, O guardian of the world! / Bestow a boon on him, O God; until then I do not seek a boon.” // 10
The Grandfather [Brahmā] said:
This is an animal, an evil-minded beast, who came here to devour you. / O goddess, his mind is not pure; he is cruel and wicked of intent. / Look at him, wicked-minded! His thought toward you does not bring welfare. (11)

Sanatkumāra said:
Then Rudrāṇī, the animator of the worlds, having heard his words, / perceived with her divine eye the audacious act committed out of ignorance: (12)
that he was previously an exclusive devotee, though tainted by the fault of his birth [as a beast]. / Having understood the matter, the daughter of Himavat then said: (13)
"O Lord, who in the worlds, being an animal, would remain motionless, / with stiffened ears and eyes, taking no food, even for a single divine day? (14)
Would anyone endure that which he has endured for a thousand / years, possessed of great splendor? He is not refined among beasts. (15)
Let him be wicked-minded or free of malice, [endowed with] great strength! / Let the boon indeed be given to him, considering that he is to be favored by me." (16)

Then that blessed god, the four-faced Grandfather, / spoke this word to the goddess, while the seers were listening: (17)
"Even thieves, through contact with noble persons in this world, might attain perfection, / just as this one, though of cruel deeds, will attain supreme perfection. (18)
Therefore, noble people should always be served, even by an evildoer; / for a man who stays near the sinless quickly attains perfection. (19)
O blameless one, this wicked-minded sinner is worthy of your favor. / Therefore, O ruler of gods, speak the boon to him that pleases you." (20)
The goddess said:
"May he be immortal, freed from old age, imperishable, and unchanging, / endowed with the power of great yoga, possessing great lordship, / a lord of gaṇas, and dear to me, if you please." (21)

Taking the cow, they were returning towards Mṛttikāvatī. / Then, because of drought, as a famine prevailed, (11) / all of them were overcome by hunger, wondering what they could eat. / When the seventh day arrived, being without food and intensely distressed, (12)
they deliberated: “Let us eat this cow; why do we sit [idle]?” / Among them, he who was named Kaṇḍara, born of the lineage of Atri, (13)
said to them: “Let us not eat this cow of our guru! / For us, O undiscerning ones, even death for the sake of the guru is praiseworthy. (14)
Let us not meet death consumed by the wrath of the guru!” / When, tormented by hunger, they did not accept that advice, (15) / he then spoke these meaningful words to them once more: / “If it has been resolved by you to eat her, O ascetics, O brahmins, (16)
let us not eat her in vain: let us consecrate her for the sake of the ancestors! / Let there not be, O fair ones, an omission here through two sins! (17)

“What has been spoken by me is the truth; that will not be false. / But those for whom you have done it will determine what is auspicious. (26)
And by no means must you remain in my presence now. / Seeing this young calf, lest I consume you [with a curse], depart!” (27)
Then, all together, deprived of awareness and bewildered, / they met their death in course of time, contemplating their teacher's word. / O Vyāsa, there is a river named Daśārṇā, auspicious with holy waters; / on its bank is a famous, radiant, divine forest.
There lived a heroic, powerful hunter named Kṣupaka. / He had sons born of Citakā, very strong indeed.
Citakā gave birth to those seven renowned sons. / They all became hunters, celebrated as the Caitakas. / Carrying bows, they wandered about killing deer and birds, / lions, tigers, elephants, and wild boars and others on every side.

Hāla was Vyāghraka, and Vidala became Śarabha; / Śaiśira was Himavat, and Hastika was Daṇḍakīlaka;
Vidarbha was Vajraka—these indeed were their names among them. / One by one, those flesh-eaters roamed the dreadful forest.
Violent, destroyers of living beings, all of them had entered a base birth. / Once, as they roamed about killing deer in that very manner,
by virtue of a good deed they reached the teacher's hermitage. / There, all the deer became agitated with fear because of them. / Noticing the terrified deer, that brahmin of very great austerities / looked in all directions and saw the hunters arriving.
Recognizing through meditation that they were his own disciples who had become hunters, / overcome with compassion, he spoke out of a desire for their well-being:

"Formerly, as brahmins, you attended upon me with respect; / yet now, because of that act and the curse resulting from the killing of the cow, / you have obtained the state of hunters here, which is contemptible and has a violent livelihood. / And that cow was eaten by you for the sake of the ancestral rites, not out of cruelty.
Therefore, fallen from here, endowed with memory of your previous lives, / having become deer on [Mount] Kālañjara, and then cakravāka birds on the lake, / and then again swans on Lake Mānasa in the island, / and having again become humans, conscious in each and every birth,
engaged in yoga, high-minded, unwearied through my grace, / freed from all sins, you shall attain the world of Brahmā."

Then, despising the act committed in their previous birth, / circumambulating [him], they went toward the Daśārṇā. / Reaching the bank of the Daśārṇā and deliberating among themselves, / remembering their previous birth, they chose death itself.
When they had made their resolve, the hunter named Arjunaka, / who had been the twice-born Kāṇḍāra, addressed them with these words:
"Gentlemen, what I said to you before was not done by you; / now that [its result] has come to pass, do not disregard my word.
I shall tell you what is beneficial; listen and do it: / let us give up this birth in such a way that we do not lose our memory.
Parents desire sons for sustenance and for being delivered [from hell]; / and we were engendered by that high-minded hunter, / and raised with hardship by our mother and likewise our father; / without asking their permission, how can we desire death?

“Afflicted with hunger today out of love for his sons, dear sons, / your father does not eat this cooked meat, nor does he drink liquor.”
Sanatkumāra said:
They too, despising their caste, though all born of sinful wombs, / addressed auspicious words to Kṣupa and to Citakā: / “May you eat without obstacle, for nourishment and for peace. / We shall not eat here today; tomorrow we will eat, without doubt.”
Then the two, being unable to endure hunger because of old age, / took their food and became completely satisfied. / But perceiving that the two were satisfied, all of them bowed their heads / and then diligently spoke these words with one accord:
“Parents, we are thoroughly disgusted with this birth. / Therefore we wish to abandon it; you should give your assent to us.”

7.6.m:
Addressed thus, he then handed me the bow with an arrow. / Aiming at the target he specified, an arrow was then shot by me. / A brahmin who lived like a deer, of steadfast vows, happened to be standing there; / struck by it, that radiant man died instantly.
Seeing him dead, I was dismissed by that king.
Out of terrible fear of the murder of a brahmin, I questioned my father. / He said: ‘You need have no fear; whence could the murder of a brahmin come upon you?
This was seen by the Self-manifest after passing through a hundred other births.’ / Then, devoted to serving my father with supreme devotion, / I lived for many years together with this wife. / Then, at some time, my father was overtaken by time.

7.6.m:
I fell from brahminhood because of sin and was born into the birth of a hunter. / I have experienced a thousand exceedingly terrible births, my sons. / But through that devotion to my father and through proper worship [of him], / my memory has not perished, my sons, and spiritual knowledge still operates.
I know you were all brahmins fallen on account of a cow / and likewise deprived of consciousness by the curse of a guru; / and later, by his command, [I know] all my sons whose minds were freed / and who have likewise regained consciousness today, O mighty ones!
And this mother of yours knows, the virtuous woman constantly devoted to her husband. / What I tell you today, do that for my pleasure.”
Then, all of you, unwearied, shall attain the highest good, / free from disease, free from sorrow, and you will not lose your consciousness.
Sons, this birth is undoubtedly my last among mortals. / Having died from here, I must go to the auspicious abode of Brahmā.

Hear from me what their names were in their existence as deer: / Dīrghajīvin, Anādhṛṣṭa, Vāyuvega, Abhikampana,
Śrīpārśva, Śaṅkhapad, and Somalakṣya as the seventh. / Remembering their previous birth and taking counsel together,
they all cast off their lives at once by leaping into the void. / Those seven, having repeatedly obtained birth among hunters and among deer,
were then born again as birds at Śaradvīpa. / Śaradvīpa is known as an auspicious lake in the Kāmpilya country.
There, too, those seven brothers were born as cakravāka birds: / Maruddeva, Śikhaṇḍin, and Rathanemisvana, / Śikhin, Jīva, Vṛkṣa, and Dhvaja—thus are they remembered.

7.6.m:
"If I were to become his son and obtain kingship, / then I would enjoy these sense-objects; of this there is no doubt."
Perceiving that thought of his, the second cakravāka, / named Śikhaṇḍin, laughed and said to him then:
"You have thought of being a prince and having kingship; / there let me be your royal priest—this is my wish as well."
Perceiving what had been thought by the two of them, Rathanemisvana then / thought: "O lord, may I be your minister there."
Sanatkumāra said:
As those three were thinking thus, the other / cakravākas, becoming enraged, spoke these words to them:
"That which should never be thought has been thought by you who desire sense-objects! / Therefore, released from here, you will attain your desire." / Having cursed them, and observing again their distressed minds— / especially the one by whom princehood and kingship were imagined—

out of compassion they spoke these words endowed with many comforting qualities / to him whose mind was bewildered, as if they themselves were afflicted with sorrow:
"By your power, O lord, we have crossed over this distress. / You gave us understanding, and you are considered our bridge.
If you had not said, 'Let the cow be offered to the ancestors,' / and had we not served our parents, we would not have had consciousness.

Then all of them, burnt by the sage’s wrath, having been hunters, deer, and cakravāka birds, / were born again in human bodies; three of them became lords of yoga in kingship. // 13 // / Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, on Kauśika’s curse in the narrative of the seven hunters, in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Those four birds, however, being teachers, by their own free will / were born again as sons of a great-souled itinerant brahmin. // 1
When they were born, that brahmin of great austerity without distress / maintained them, preceded by their good fortune. // 2 // / Having observed the Vedic vows and studied the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, / they devoted themselves solely to yoga, steadfast in it and focused entirely on it. // 3
The other three also, O Vyāsa, impelled by their own past action, / attained that birth which had previously been conceived by them. // 4
The first was indeed born from Aṇuha, remembered as Brahmadatta. / One was the son of Aṇuha, the second was of his domestic priest, // 5

Aṇuha gave the abundant kingdom to Brahmadatta / and then, together with Kīrtimatī, he went to the forest. // 8 // / The sovereign domestic priest, Dhṛtarāta, having installed his son / in his own duty, then, having observed his vows, departed for Pañcāla. // 9
The minister Sudhanvan, having installed in his own office his son, / the unfailing Brahmadhanvan, departed together with his wife. // 10 // / When they had gone to their own realms, the majestic Brahmadatta / ruled the kingdom together with Pañcāla and Brahmadhanvan. // 11
While he ruled the kingdom, sacrificing and enjoying pleasures, / many years passed happily for the meritorious king. // 12
Then, after a long time, together with his wife and companions, / he stayed happily in his palace, like Kubera in the Puṣpaka aerial chariot. // 13

7.6.m:
At that very time, the four auspicious brahmins, / endowed with great yoga, spoke thus to one another: // 21 // / “Our purpose is fulfilled; what purpose is there in staying here in human birth? / Let us go to our own Brahma-origin; let us be freed from this great danger. // 22
And those three companions of ours in vows are languishing; / let us awaken them here, so that they may not suffer ruin.” // 23
Then all those twice-born ones bowed to their father and said: / “Dear father, we are masters of yoga, perfected indeed by our own past deed. // 24
We take our leave: we shall go to our own origin fashioned by Brahmā. / Having cast off these human bodies, do not grieve; dismiss us; salutation to you!” // 25

Then, having assumed their postures, those whose wealth was austerity, being concentrated in yoga, departed. / And their father of great splendor saw them transformed into light. // 32
Taking the letter and meditating upon his sons, / he went swiftly to Kāmpilya, desiring to see the best of kings. // 33
And that king, having arrived from the Śāla forest, was entering the city; / and the brahmin showed him the letter from afar. // 34

he received the letter and read it attentively. / And there were two verses in that letter conferring good fortune: // 37
"Those who, afflicted by the curse pronounced by their guru for the slaughter of a cow, / through devotion to their father attained knowledge and were all born with auspicious destinies: // 38
Seven hunters in Daśārṇa, deer on mount Kālañjara, / cakravāka birds on Śaradvīpa, geese on Lake Mānasa; // 39

Sanatkumāra said:

Indeed, gods and siddhas along with cāraṇas declare her / to be peerless in beauty among other women across the three worlds, a lovely lady.
And he did not find an opportunity with her and her husband: / at what time would there be her separation from her husband?
Hearing of her as exceedingly beautiful and chaste, that Brahmadhanvan, / longing for her separation from her husband, assumed the form of a tiger.
And having assumed an immense, deformed, and terrifying form then, / he frightened the deer by his sight, O Vyāsa, very foolishly.
Then, O Lord, that herd of deer, terrified by fear of the tiger, / rushed out of sight with a speed resembling thought and wind.
Desiring his life, Hāla too fled then with the deer; / that brahmin woman Sudharmā also, the lovely woman, out of fear of the tiger,

In the meantime, that Brahmadhanvan took her by the hand, / and delighted, said this to her: “Why do you ponder in your heart?
Will you not embrace me today, who have escaped from the jaws of death? / Am I not indeed your beloved husband? Do not be angry, O fair-complexioned lady!”
Then, out of wickedness, he kissed her on the cheek; / and embracing her, the evil-minded one pressed his limbs against her limbs.
He unfastened the knot of her garment and forcibly drank from her lower lip. / And by that act, the fair lady recognized that he was wicked.
Sudharmā said:
“You are not my husband, fool! You are Śakra, there is no doubt about this! / I am not an object for love once more, O very evil-minded one!”
Addressed thus by her and cast off on every side, / he fell onto the surface of the earth and assumed his own form.

Having cursed that cruel man, the resolute lady of noble conduct / went toward those deer, and then she saw her husband.
He too, tormented by sorrow and thinking that she was killed, / saw her while lamenting, and embracing her, spoke these words:
"By good fortune you have returned, escaped from the jaws of death! / Surely you were not seen by that king of beasts, auspicious lady?" / Sudharmā said:
"That evil-minded one was no lion; he was someone capable of changing form at will. / Arriving for my sake, he was burned by me like a moth. / By my curse that wicked-souled one acquired the nature of a tiger, / just as King Saudāsa assumed a demon's body through the curse of Śakti."
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard her words, Hāla, who knew the true nature of dharma and wealth, / saw through his divine eye the imperishable Brahmadhanvan.

7.6.m:
There was an exceedingly righteous seer named Bhalandana, / learned and compassionate, standing firm like the earth.
His wife was named Ṛk, born of Vasiṣṭha's lineage, possessing auspicious marks, / peerless in beauty, virtuous, so that nowhere was any woman equal to her, / devoted to her husband, highly fortunate, supreme among knowers of all dharmas. / For her there was no other deity on earth except her husband.
Once the gods saw that lotus-eyed woman; / maddened by her beauty and virtues, they could not individually find composure. / Nor was she able to be obtained by messengers, nor by deeds, / nor by gifts, nor by honors, nor by force, nor by service.
Fire seized the auspicious woman as she had entered and was standing in the fire-sanctuary. / But she did not say, 'I am yours,' nor did she say, 'I am not yours.'
She had no anger, nor pride, nor self-conceit, nor envy; / nothing was dear to her except that she thought only of her husband.

7.6.m:
Because his power of assuming forms at will was always derived from me, / for that very reason he shall attain well-being again through my grace.
Sanatkumāra said:
O Vyāsa, that wicked-souled one, fond of the hermitage of Viśvāmitra, / who had always dwelled in the primeval forest, was made the leader of the Gaṇas by the goddess.
Whoever retains this māhātmya of his or recites it / constantly to a brahmin, O Vyāsa, shall attain mastery over yoga.
This must be studied until the end by those desiring sovereignty in yoga; / attaining another birth, they achieve it without doubt.
And if a restrained, pure, and single-minded human being hears this constantly, / O dear boy, through his accumulated merit that man gains a form like that of Śakra.
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.6.m:
Reflecting upon some knower of scriptures, as a scholar of scripture seeks an object, / and repeatedly contemplating the joy born of obtaining a son,
abundant water, exceedingly cool and fragrant, / fell into the lake and became pure through her radiance, / just as knowledge is imparted to a disciple by an intellectual teacher through mental capacity.
Plunging into that lake of spotless water, the goddess / shone like the blazing splendor of the sun standing in the midst of the sky. / Plunging in, the sinless one then shed her black sheath; / freed from it, she shone like the moon at the passing of the dark clouds.
From that sheath of hers arose Kauśikī, renowned throughout the worlds, / as formerly night arose from the body of the Creator who desired to create the universe. / She had lips like bimba fruit, sharp and very beautiful teeth, a charming face like the serene moon, / well-formed, dark, wavy, long hair, and a slight line of upright hair.

7.6.m:
With well-proportioned lotus-like feet, a deep navel whirling to the right, / concealed knee-bones and veins, and shapely ankles, she was like Lakṣmī without a lotus.
Gracious in form, with nascent breasts, eyes charming as blossoming blue lotuses, / that slender-waisted one was adorned with fine ornaments made of excellent diamonds and gems.
Wearing armlets, having bracelets bound on, her radiance illuminated by bangles, / that undefeated one bore eight arms equipped with weapons. / Having finger-guards of monitor-lizard skin tied on, she wore splendid armor, / radiant, inborn, and impenetrable even by the gods and asuras together with Indra.

7.6.m:
Devoid of old age and death, free from grief and suffering, / you will possess great yoga and be invincible in battles. / You will go into renown in the world under the name of Kauśikī, / and by other praiseworthy names based upon your virtues and deeds.
Those devotees of yours who remember you when trapped in difficulties / will cross over perils, O fair-faced one, by your grace. / 'Excellent one, most desirable, granter of boons, Durgā, accomplisher of all ends'— / thus sages will continually praise you with divine names.
With mutterings of prayers, bowings, fire offerings, and various gifts, / living beings will always worship you on earth.
Then the goddess created a chariot yoked with lions, radiant as the sun, / furnished with flags and adorned with a network of tinkling bells; / and she assigned the Vindhya, best of mountains, for her dwelling.
Sanatkumāra said:
Being thus addressed, that goddess bowed to the Mistress of the Universe / and mounted the divine, auspicious chariot made of gold.

With the cries of birds, as though with a welcome, the Vindhya / then honored that immeasurable, sinless Kauśikī who had arrived there,

7.6.m:
The goddess chose for her dwelling the peak of the mountain, / blossoming and resounded by flocks of birds nested in trees,
with grassy slopes of green stones moistened by the spray of cascades, / its breeze made fragrant by blossoms of various trees and creepers,
its lofty, broad ridges and outlying peaks strewn / with streams of cascade-waters cold with masses of snow; / and on that summit of the best of mountains the goddess took up her abode,
where impassioned bees clung to branches of flowering trees. / Whoever recites this regularly, or listens with concentrated mind / to the complete manifestation of Kauśikī, attains the supreme state.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, named 'The Manifestation of Kauśikī', in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sanatkumāra said:
Then, having dispatched that Kauśikī thither, the daughter of the Himavat / ceased from her severe austerity and performed her ritual ablution according to rule. / [Apparatus notes]

Wearing two white garments, adorned with divine garlands and unguents, / she looked at the mountain beside her and said, 'I shall grant you a boon.'
When the goddess had spoken thus, the mountain assumed an embodied form, / bowed down, and chose a boon: 'May there be your presence upon me, / and may my name, marked by your name, become renowned / through all the worlds by your grace, O Great Goddess!'
Agni also chose a boon from the boon-granter: 'O goddess, do not be angry with me.' / And the trees there chose to bear flowers and fruit forever. / 'Be very gracious to us, and may we have devotion toward you'— / thus all the female attendants then chose [boons] from the goddess.
Being worshipped by many deities, the daughter of the king of mountains / shone, surpassing other splendors, like solar radiance.

Even while abiding in her husband's heart, and her husband abiding in hers, / that daughter of the mountain-king thought: 'I am separated.' / Then she, the giver of boons, set out to see her husband, the granter of boons, / the abode of all splendors, the lord of the whole universe.
Saluted by the forest-deities of that place, having circumambulated the kindled fire, / having bowed to the most venerable seers and shown respect to their venerable folk, / the sustainer of the world then flew up into the sky together with Somanandin, / with the lion, with the gaṇas, and with her retinue.

Dispersing masses of clouds in the sky by her own splendor,
fanned by breezes cool with droplets of icy water, / that daughter of the mountain-king, remembering only her husband,
swiftly came to the side of the one who burned the god of love. / Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter in the Skandapurāṇa.
Sūta said:
Then Vyāsa, with folded hands, said to that son of Brahmā: / 'For what reason was Kauśikī dispatched by the goddess to the Vindhya at that time?' / Thus addressed then by Vyāsa, the wise son of Brahmā / began to relate everything just as it had happened in the past.
'Desiring to propitiate the goddess, the Vindhya performed austerity in ancient times; / then Pārvatī, being pleased, said to the Vindhya: "I shall grant you a boon." / "May you dwell upon me forever"—thus he who obstructed the sun / requested of the daughter of the mountain-king, and she replied: "So be it."'

7.6.m:
Dividing her own body into two, like a blazing flame of fire, / she dispatched Kauśikī from herself to burn the lords of the dānavas.
Then the best of sages spoke to that son of Brahmā: / "O highly wise one, why was Mount Vindhya an obstructer of the sun?"
Questioned by the wise Vyāsa, Sanatkumāra spoke: / "Listen to why Mount Vindhya became an obstructer of the sun.
In former times, Vindhya said to the sun: 'Why do you not circumambulate me / as you do Mount Meru? What disregard have you toward me, O lord?'

He then said to Vindhya: 'Indeed, it cannot be done thus.' / Rejected by the sun, Mount Vindhya expanded; / standing blocking his path, he thus became an obstructer of the sun.

7.6.m:
Then, with the light lost in the world, the gods, agitated in their minds, / approached Agastya and spoke these words with composed minds:
'Mount Vindhya stands obstructing the sun's path. / Hold him back, O highly wise one; you are always our refuge.'
Then Agastya of great austerities, going to the mountain, spoke thus: / 'I shall travel to the southern quarter; grant me a passage, O mountain.
You ought to remain [as you are] until I return.' / And from that time onward, the sage's return never came to pass.
Then Vyāsa questioned that lord, the son of the Grandsire: / 'Kauśikī was sent to Vindhya to destroy the dānavas.
Who were they, whose [sons were they], or for what reason were the dānavas slain by Kauśikī? / You ought to tell me all this in brief, O sage.'

7.6.m:
The wise son of the Grandsire, thus urged by Vyāsa, / began to explain this question in brief:
'In ancient times, in a past, most wonderful battle between gods and asuras, / Sunda and Upasunda were the two sons of Niśumbha.
Hearing that all their kinsmen had been slain by the gods in the great battle, / they became enraged at the gods, bellowing like bulls,
like two mighty lions whose weapon-like claws and fangs had been wrenched away, / hissing fiercely with venom like two serpents with broken fangs.
Unable to fight the gods, their faction destroyed, those two great asuras, / mighty in strength, were enraged like two Suparṇas whose wings had been clipped.

[…] and these two sons went toward Gokarṇa, / wishing to worship the god Brahmā, being endowed with boundless splendor.
Then Vyāsa spoke: 'Tell me about Gokarṇa: / in what country, for what purpose, or by whom was it produced in ancient times?'
The son of Brahmā, thus urged by Vyāsa, said: / 'Listen, my child, to the sacred origin of Gokarṇa in brief:
When his eldest son Triśiras had been slain by the Wielder of the Thunderbolt, / Tvaṣṭṛ, that treasury of austerities, then produced a son named Vṛtra:
long-armed, round-faced, with a thick and broad chest, / well-knit knees and jaw, with a voice roaring like a rain-cloud,
with handsome eyes, good flanks, a fine waist, long red-rimmed eyes, / a conqueror of all the gods in battle, unconquered.
Having conquered all the immortals, that one of great splendor swallowed Indra. / Then a yawn created by the great seers entered him.

7.6.m:
Then, as he was yawning, the performer of a hundred sacrifices emerged quickly / from his mouth, contracting his own body by means of yogamāyā.
Seeing his power of yoga, his vigor, and his heroism in battle, / all the gods, terrified, went to Brahmā for refuge.
Seeing the immortals who were thus afraid of that enemy of the gods, / the Grandsire, lord of creatures, born from the lotus, quickly spoke:
'I know that you have been defeated by Vṛtra at the head of the battle. / I see no means by which he may be conquered in fight.
Let us all go together to see the god, the lord of Umā, / the lord of the universe, the creator, the granter of boons, who is tender to devotees.

That lord, Śambhu, Mahādeva, the great yogin, / propitiated by our prostrations, devotion, and praise, will bring about peace.'
Then all the gods arose, wishing to see the god of gods, / and not seeing him, they roamed the earth with its oceans and mountains.
Then Viṣṇu, the great yogin, saw the goddess, the daughter of Himavat, / sitting in the form of a child, her limbs smeared with dust,
like the fresh crescent of the moon, like the morning radiance of the sun, / like a slender flame of fire when offered with oblation.
Recognizing through yoga the sovereign of the gods who possesses great yoga, / Viṣṇu, the victorious lord of the world, praised Pārvatī:
Viṣṇu spoke:
"You are the creator of all beings, you are the destroyer, O queen of the gods! / You are the supporter of this world, eternal, imperishable Prakṛti.
You are radiance, the night, moonlight, renown, contentment, Umā, fortitude, / intellect, intelligence, memory, discernment, twilight, splendor, praise, and thought.

7.6.m:
You are the ruler, O goddess, of the gods, mother of the gaṇas, motherly ruler of the gaṇas, / Bhadrakālī, Mahāgaurī, Kauśikī, who dwells on the Vindhya,
Durgā, Khyāti, Mahāvidyā, Gāyatrī, you are Sarasvatī, / Svāhā, Svadhā, Mahāmāyā, Lakṣmī, the mistress of the lords of yoga.
[You are] the meteor, Satī, daughter of the mountain, Maitreyī, the celibate student, / the ascetic woman, Revatī, Ṣaṣṭhī, granter of thousands of boons and lesser boons. // With teeth, brows, eyes, voice, and hands, O sovereign goddess, / you equal jasmine, a bow, a deer, a cuckoo, and sprouts of the aśoka tree.
With your gait, eyes, and radiant splendor, O goddess, / you forever surpass the rutting elephant, the blooming blue lotus, and the full moon.

7.6.m:
Your speech is sweet and indistinguishable like that of an intoxicated cuckoo; your lovely hair is black like a swarm of bees; / with breasts swelling like clusters of blossoming flowers, you shine like a wish-fulfilling creeper in bloom.
O goddess, you are unceasingly saluted with devotion in heaven by goddesses; / you are constantly worshipped, O daughter of the mountain, upon mountain summits by sages.
You are always worshipped with heaps of fragrant flowers by Gandharvas; / having attained the path of the wind, O sinless one, you are praised upon your arrival.
Mounted upon a lion with tossing tawny mane, you shine / like the radiant, brilliant sunrise standing upon the peak of Mount Meru.
Desiring to slay the Daityas in battle with streams of straight-flying arrows, you shine / like the form of the sun dispelling the darkness with its rays.
Holding up a sharp axe in the clash between gods and Dānavas, / enraged, O goddess, you shine as though tearing apart heaven and earth.
Then, casting off childhood, she assumed another form, / as if a union of all splendors unified in the sky:

Then Śarva, invisible, spoke to those best of gods: / “Tell me, O best of gods, for what purpose you have come.”
Then Brahmā said to the supreme lord, whose emblem is the bull: / “Having slain Vṛtra, let Purandara regain his kingdom.”

Having gone there, a man who bows down to Maheśvara with devotion / attains [the fruit of] a horse sacrifice and is freed from all sins.

7.6.m:
Then those two Dānavas, O Vyāsa, went to Gokarṇa; / there they performed extremely fierce austerity, subsisting on water and air.
After some time, having recognized their fierce austerity, / Brahmā, worshipped by the gods, approached them.
Then the two mighty-armed ones saw Brahmā, the grandfather, / the supporter of the universe, four-faced, standing before them,
clad in white garments, radiant, adorned with white garlands and ointments, / a consolidated brilliance unbearable to look upon, like that of suns.
Then the grandfather said: “I am pleased with you two, my sons, / by this fierce austerity. Choose the desired boon.”
Bowing to the grandfather, they two chose immortality. / Brahmā then said: “Immortality is not possible except for gods.
Death must inevitably come to both of you from some single cause.” / Then they chose immortality except through slaying each other.
Saying, "So be it," the Grandfather, having granted that boon to both of them, / went to his own abode in a chariot drawn by swans.

Then, in the formidable, beautiful city, to the assembly hall named Kāntā, / the assembled lords of the dānavas came with contented minds. / In it, upon a distinguished, spacious, excellent seat of gold, / the mighty-armed Sunda, best of the dānavas, sat down.
Then Nisunda occupied another, auspicious [seat] adorned with gold and gems; / then the wise Maya sat upon one made of gold.
And the other dānavas then took seats, O sage— / variegated with gold and gems, radiant and large.
That assembly hall shone there with the assembled lords of the dānavas, / like the sky at the dissolution [of the universe] with clouds bearing cranes and lightning flashes.
Then, raising his head that was like a halo of gem-rays, / Sunda spoke this word, with a deep, pleasing voice like a raincloud:
"O lords of the dānavas, I shall wipe away the tears of all [of you], / having conquered Indra together with the gods in the forefront of battle. / Let us march, all armored! Be ready, O dānavas, / with raised weapons in hand, to conquer the three worlds!"

Hearing that speech of his, Prabhu said to the lord of the asuras: / "Through sacrifices, vows, austerities, and restraints, the enemies of the asuras
are constantly invigorated with zeal by the varnas and ashrams on earth. / Having slain them first, we shall then conquer the gods."
Hearing that speech of his, the best of the dānavas said: / "Having first destroyed their source of revenue, we shall then conquer the immortals."
Then Dhundhu, whose voice was like clouds and kettle-drums, said: / "This world merely follows its king; how can the sinless be killed?
In the past, the kingdom was taken from us by the gods after slaying our people; / having conquered solely by prowess, the kingdom of the daityas was seized by the gods.

Likewise, from them in a battle thick with raised banners, we too / shall bring back Fortune, whose eyes are agitated, having conquered [them] in combat.
When an offense is equal, the blazing fiery spirit of high-minded beings / naturally unfolds, always directed against the powerful alone."
Then Mura, whose sound was like a drum, having heard the words of Dhundhu, / threw his head high and said, as if laughing:
"Formerly, there were high-souled lords of the dānavas endowed with great strength: / Hiraṇyakaśipu, Vṛtra, Prahlāda, Namuci, Bali,
and millions of other dānavas of great courage and great strength, / by whom Fortune was forcibly made to dwell upon their chests.
Now that you are few in remnant, O best of asuras, / how can the kingdom be recovered by conquering the gods in combat? / Seek to obtain the kingdom quickly by some other means / that achieves the desired goal without conflict with place and time."
Hearing that statement then, the great asura Aṃśumālī / spoke this sweet, gentle word that conformed to practical purpose:

Sanatkumāra said:
Then the army of the chiefs of the Dānavas set forth to destroy the world, / crowded with rutting elephants and surrounded by chariots and horses.
That army of the Dānavas then spread in every direction, / like the water of the ocean stirred up by the wind at the dissolution [of the world]. // Some slew the brahmins, some crushed the Vaiśyas, / others overpowered the Kṣatriyas, and others devoured the Śūdras.

7.6.m:
The enemies of the immortals swallowed down, licked up, roared, and broke in pieces everywhere / the food at sacrifices, the eaters of oblation, and the sacrificial posts.
Resounding with the recitation of properly studied Vedas, their shrubs and trees frequented by eminent sages, / with abundant heaps of bark garments, black antelope skins, and darbha grass, with cool mountain torrents flowing abundantly at their margins, // filled at their edges with wild rice and gavedhuka grass, with deer, bears, and monkeys sleeping in trust, / shrouded with canopies of smoke from the sacrificial fire—other [demons] spread out and utterly destroyed the hermitages.
Seizing the sages' matted locks, which shone like the skins of old serpents / and had been washed with the water of sacred fords, some Asuras tore them out. // 110 ...ttamāṅgo (? .
